```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 18))
set.seed(313)
# cividis: navy, slate, gray, khaki, gold, yellow (viridisLite::cividis(9)[c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9)])
navy <- "#00204D"; slate <- "#414D6B"; cgray <- "#7C7B78"; khaki <- "#9B9477"; gold <- "#BCAF6F"; yellow <- "#FFEA46"
two <- c(navy, gold)               # the two groups, wherever there are two
# charts on dark (.inverse) slides: white text on the navy background, yellow and gold for the two groups
dark <- theme(text = element_text(color = "white"), axis.text = element_text(color = "white"),
              legend.text = element_text(color = "white"), plot.title = element_text(color = "white"),
              panel.grid.major = element_line(color = slate), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
              plot.background = element_rect(fill = navy, color = NA),
              panel.background = element_rect(fill = navy, color = NA),
              legend.background = element_rect(fill = navy, color = NA),
              legend.key = element_rect(fill = navy, color = NA))
two_dark <- c(yellow, gold)

# Causal graphs. Nodes are letters in circles, or words in boxes (boxes = TRUE).
# A node's size is fixed on the page, in inches, while the figure's size decides how
# many inches a data unit is. draw_dag measures both on the graphics device open when it
# is called (in a rendered document, the chunk's figure) and stops every arrow `gap`
# inches short of the two nodes it joins. Arrows listed in `dashed` are dashed; arrows
# listed in `highlight` are gold. One panel per value of `panel`.
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, dashed = character(0), highlight = character(0), boxes = FALSE,
                     text_size = 7, xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.4), strip_size = 18,
                     gap = 0.05) {
  if (!"panel" %in% names(nodes)) { nodes$panel <- ""; edges$panel <- "" }
  pad <- unit(0.35, "lines"); border <- 0.5; dot <- 16; stroke <- 0.8; lw <- c(black = 0.7, gold = 1.5)
  p <- ggplot() +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = strip_size), panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
  p <- if (boxes) {
    p + geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, label.size = border,
                   label.padding = pad)
  } else {
    p + geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y), size = dot, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = stroke) +
      geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, parse = TRUE)
  }
  # Inches per data unit: the panels share what the strips and spacing leave of the figure.
  inch <- function(u, f) f(u, "in", valueOnly = TRUE)
  g <- ggplotGrob(p)
  pp <- ggplot_build(p)$layout$panel_params[[1]]
  per_unit <- min((dev.size("in")[1] - sum(inch(g$widths, grid::convertWidth))) /
                    (length(unique(nodes$panel)) * diff(pp$x.range)),
                  (dev.size("in")[2] - sum(inch(g$heights, grid::convertHeight))) / diff(pp$y.range))
  # Half the width and half the height of each node, outline included, in data units.
  if (boxes) {
    text <- lapply(as.character(nodes$name), grid::textGrob, gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = text_size * .pt))
    nodes$hw <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobWidth(t), grid::convertWidth)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertWidth) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
    nodes$hh <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobHeight(t), grid::convertHeight)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertHeight) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  } else {
    # R draws a circle of radius 0.375 times its font size (shape 21)
    nodes$hw <- nodes$hh <- (0.375 * (dot * .pt + stroke * .stroke / 2) / 72 +
                               stroke * .stroke / 2 / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  }
  e <- edges |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "from" = "name")) |>
    rename(x0 = x, y0 = y, hw0 = hw, hh0 = hh) |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "to" = "name")) |>
    mutate(dx = x - x0, dy = y - y0, len = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2), ux = dx / len, uy = dy / len,
           col = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% highlight, "#BCAF6F", "black"),
           style = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% dashed, "dashed", "solid"),
           # the start clears the node by gap; the end by gap and half the arrow's line width,
           # which the rounded tip adds
           g0 = gap / per_unit,
           g1 = (gap + ifelse(col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]) * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit,
           # distance from a node's center, along the arrow, to the node's outline grown by g
           s0 = if (boxes) pmin((hw0 + g0) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh0 + g0) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw0 + g0,
           s1 = if (boxes) pmin((hw + g1) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh + g1) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw + g1,
           xs = x0 + s0 * ux, ys = y0 + s0 * uy, xe = x - s1 * ux, ye = y - s1 * uy)
  p + geom_segment(data = e, aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye, linetype = style, color = col),
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"),
                   linewidth = ifelse(e$col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_linetype_identity() + scale_color_identity()
}
```

# Part 1: Normative and applied ethics

## Normative ethics: four frameworks

::: {.notes}
They read these: one line each. The consequentialist's difficulty is the one this course can help with.
:::

| | judges an action by | a difficulty |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Consequentialism | its effects | predicting consequences |
| Deontology | whether it follows a rule or a duty | a rule kept where it leads somewhere terrible |
| Virtue ethics | the character it expresses | virtues conflict |
| Pragmatic ethics | norms held like hypotheses, revised by inquiry | how people judge, or how they should? |

These approaches are not mutually exclusive or exhaustive, so we do not have to choose one of them or limit our thinking to using only these ideas.

::: {.source}
ms4ds, section 3.2.2 (the last line) and sections 3.2.2.1 to 3.2.2.3 (the first three rows); Wikipedia, Deontology and Pragmatic ethics.
:::

## Which framework?

::: {.notes}
Pairs, two minutes, then hands for each argument. Then ask which of the four would need data to settle, and what kind of data.
:::

A hospital is deciding whether to use a model to choose which patients get a follow-up call after discharge.

1. "A good doctor would not hand that judgment to a score."
2. "Use it. In the pilot, readmissions fell."
3. "Try it on one ward, watch what happens, and change the rules as we learn."
4. "Don't. Patients never agreed to their records being used this way."

::: {.ask}
Which framework is each argument using? Which of them would you need data to settle?
:::

## Consequentialism

::: {.notes}
"Than any available alternative": a comparison between actions, only one of which is taken. ms4ds goes on: an observational model does not tell us what an intervention would bring about.
:::

> An act is right "if and only if the act [...] will produce, will probably produce, or is intended to produce, a greater balance of good over evil than any available alternative."

::: {.source}
Wikipedia, Consequentialism.
:::

```{r alternatives, fig.height=2.1, fig.alt="A choice branches into the action taken, whose consequences are seen, and an alternative, drawn dashed, whose consequences are never seen."}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("choice", "action taken", "alternative", "consequences seen", "never seen"),
                    x = c(0, 1.9, 1.9, 4.2, 4.2), y = c(0.5, 1, 0, 1, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("choice", "choice", "action taken", "alternative"),
                    to = c("action taken", "alternative", "consequences seen", "never seen")),
         dashed = c("choice alternative", "alternative never seen"),
         boxes = TRUE, text_size = 6, xlim = c(-0.8, 5.5), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3))
```

Causal understanding is necessary to apply consequentialism.

::: {.source}
ms4ds, section 3.4.
:::

## Utilitarianism

::: {.notes}
Bentham and Mill. Everyone's happiness counts, and nobody's counts for more. Then each difficulty and what it is in data science.
:::

Bentham and Mill: choose the action that does the most good, adding up everyone's happiness.

| a difficulty | in data science |
|:---|:---|
| defining utility | choosing the outcome, the metric or the loss |
| trading off between people | adding gains and losses across people |
| judging acts or rules | one decision, or the model that makes them all |
| predicting consequences | effects of actions, not associations |

::: {.source}
ms4ds, section 3.2.2.1 (the four difficulties); Wikipedia, Consequentialism.
:::

## Utilitarian language

::: {.notes}
Pairs, two minutes; two pairs report. If a pair is stuck: an A/B test that keeps whichever version has the higher average time in the app.
:::

Data science is usually framed (perhaps implicitly) as utilitarian because of its focus on prediction/causation (consequences) and optimization (utility).

::: {.source}
ms4ds, section 3.2.2, discussion questions.
:::

::: {.ask}
Choose a data science task: a recommender, a credit score, an A/B test. Say it in utilitarian language: whose good, measured how, added up over who? Then give one objection a deontologist or a virtue ethicist would make.
:::

## The Belmont and Menlo principles

::: {.notes}
The history in one breath: Tuskegee, 1932 to 1972; the National Research Act, 1974; the report, 1978. Beneficence is the consequentialist clause.
:::

```{r belmont_timeline, fig.height=2.0, fig.alt="A timeline. A dark bar marks the Tuskegee study, 1932 to 1972; dots mark the National Research Act in 1974, the Belmont Report in 1978 (respect for persons, beneficence, justice) and the Menlo Report in 2012 (adds respect for law and the public interest)."}
lab <- data.frame(
  x     = c(1975.5, 1976.5, 1976.5, 2013.5, 2013.5),
  y     = c(0.3, -0.3, -0.68, 0.86, 0.3),
  label = c("1974 National Research Act", "1978 Belmont Report", "respect for persons, beneficence, justice",
            "2012 Menlo Report", "adds respect for law\nand the public interest"),
  hj    = c(1, 0, 0, 1, 1), vj = c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0),
  bold  = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))
ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 1928, xend = 2018, y = 0, yend = 0, color = cgray, linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1932, xmax = 1972, ymin = -0.17, ymax = 0.17, fill = navy) +
  annotate("text", x = 1952, y = 0, label = "Tuskegee study, 1932 to 1972", color = "white", size = 5.2) +
  annotate("point", x = c(1974, 1978, 2012), y = 0, size = 4.5, color = gold) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(x, y, label = label, hjust = hj, vjust = vj,
                            fontface = ifelse(bold, "bold", "plain"), color = ifelse(bold, navy, "black")),
            size = 5, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1928, 2018), ylim = c(-1.05, 1.35), clip = "off") +
  theme_void()
```

In the Tuskegee study, Black men with syphilis were never told they had it and were kept from treatment after penicillin was known to work.

> Beneficence, in the Menlo Report's words: "Do not harm; Maximize probable benefits and minimize probable harms; Systematically assess both risk of harm and benefit."

::: {.source}
ms4ds, section 3.3.1, which quotes the Menlo Report (2012); Wikipedia, Belmont Report.
:::

## The five Cs

::: {.notes}
A checklist for data practice. Consent is part of Belmont's respect for persons, as ms4ds notes. The class uses these in discussion 3.
:::

| | asks |
|:---|:---|
| Consent | did people explicitly agree, knowing what will be collected and what for? |
| Clarity | do they understand what their consent allows? |
| Consistency and trust | does the system behave as people expect? |
| Control and transparency | can they see the status of their data, and opt in or out of particular uses later? |
| Consequences | what unintended harm could the data do, to children for example, or by linking sources to identify people? |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

::: {.source}
Loukides, Mason and Patil, *Ethics and Data Science*, as summarized in ms4ds, section 3.3.2.
:::

# Part 2: Causal models

## Observational studies that recommend a practice {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: most observational studies that recommend a practice do not ask for a trial first.
:::

```{r prasad, fig.height=3, fig.alt="Bars: 298 observational studies; 167 of them recommended a medical practice; 24 of those said a randomized trial should come first."}
prasad <- data.frame(label = c("observational studies", "recommended a practice", "of those, asked for a trial first"),
                     n = c(298, 167, 24))
prasad$label <- factor(prasad$label, levels = rev(prasad$label))
ggplot(prasad, aes(n, label, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.25, color = "white", size = 8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c(cgray, gold, yellow), levels(prasad$label)[3:1])) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 360), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  dark +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 20, color = "white"), plot.margin = margin(5, 40, 5, 5))
```

::: {.source style="color: #BCAF6F"}
Prasad, Jorgenson, Ioannidis and Cifu (2013), *Journal of Clinical Epidemiology* 66, 361--366: the 298 eligible observational studies among the 631 original articles of 2010 in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, *Lancet*, *JAMA* and *Annals of Internal Medicine*.
:::

## Structural causal models

::: {.notes}
The reading's definition. Three shapes; a common cause is the usual source of confounding.
:::

> "a sequence of assignments for generating a joint distribution starting from independent noise variables."

```{r three_shapes, fig.height=2.6}
shapes <- c("fork", "chain", "collider")
nodes <- data.frame(panel = rep(shapes, each = 3),
                    name = c("Z", "X", "Y", "M", "X", "Y", "C", "X", "Y"),
                    x = rep(c(1, 0, 2), 3), y = rep(c(1, 0, 0), 3))
edges <- data.frame(panel = rep(shapes, each = 2),
                    from = c("Z", "Z", "X", "M", "X", "Y"),
                    to = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "C", "C"))
nodes$panel <- factor(nodes$panel, levels = shapes); edges$panel <- factor(edges$panel, levels = shapes)
draw_dag(nodes, edges)
```

$Z$ a common cause, $M$ a mediator, $C$ a common effect.

::: {.source}
fairmlbook, chapter 5, "Causal models" and "Causal graphs."
:::

## Exercise, weight and heart disease

::: {.notes}
The reading's first example. Alone, then compare with a neighbor. Both numbers from the room before the next slide.
:::

$U_1 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(1/2)$, $\;U_2, U_3 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(1/3)$, independent; $\mathrm{Ber}(q)$ is 1 with probability $q$.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
1. $X := U_1$ (exercise)
2. $W :=$ if $X = 1$ then $0$ else $U_2$ (overweight)
3. $H :=$ if $X = 1$ then $0$ else $U_3$ (heart disease)
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
```{r program_dag, fig.width=3, fig.height=2}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("X", "W", "H"), x = c(1, 0, 2), y = c(1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("X", "X"), to = c("W", "H")), ylim = c(-0.35, 1.35))
```
:::
::::

Apart from the noise, an arrow into a variable comes from each variable its line uses: $W$ and $H$ are both computed from $X$.

::: {.ask}
Compute $P(H = 1)$ and $P(H = 1 \mid W = 1)$.
:::

::: {.source}
fairmlbook, chapter 5, "A first example."
:::

## Conditioning and intervening

::: {.notes}
Overweight people have twice the population's rate. Intervening replaces the line for W, which deletes the arrow into W; H is unchanged. Definition of confounded from the reading.
:::

$P(H = 1) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac13 = \tfrac16$, $\qquad P(H = 1 \mid W = 1) = \tfrac13$.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
$do(W := 1)$: replace line 2 by $W := 1$. In the graph, the arrow into $W$ is deleted.

$P(H = 1 \mid do(W := 1)) = \tfrac16$.
:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
```{r program_do, fig.width=3, fig.height=1.8}
draw_dag(data.frame(panel = "after do(W := 1)", name = c("X", "W", "H"), x = c(1, 0, 2), y = c(1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(panel = "after do(W := 1)", from = "X", to = "H"), strip_size = 22,
         ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3))
```
:::
::::

> "The substitution $W := 1$ does not correspond to a conditioning on $W = 1$. One is an action, albeit inconsequential in this case."

$X$ and $Y$ are **confounded** when $P(Y = y \mid do(X := x)) \ne P(Y = y \mid X = x)$.

::: {.source}
fairmlbook, chapter 5, "A first example" and "Confounding."
:::

## The average treatment effect

::: {.notes}
A population quantity. "This policy causes better outcomes" is a claim about something like it. Effects can vary a lot between people; the next slide shows it.
:::

$$
\text{ATE} = E[Y \mid do(X := 1)] - E[Y \mid do(X := 0)]
$$

$X$ set to 1 for everyone, against $X$ set to 0 for everyone, with the arrows into $X$ deleted.

$$
E[Y \mid X = 1] - E[Y \mid X = 0]
$$

The observed difference: the people who happened to be treated, against those who were not.

> "Causal effects are population quantities."

::: {.source}
fairmlbook, chapter 5, "Causal effects."
:::

## Adding up over people

::: {.notes}
Both conditions matter: gains that add up, and no interference. The bars are imagined: no one's own effect is observed. Answer to listen for: the effects within groups defined before treatment.
:::

If gains add up across people, and nobody's outcome depends on anyone else's treatment, treating all $n$ rather than none changes the expected total by $n \times \text{ATE}$: the utilitarian's comparison.

```{r gains, fig.height=2, fig.alt="Bars for ten imagined people: seven gain between 1 and 4, three lose between 1 and 3; a dashed line marks the average, 1."}
gains <- data.frame(person = factor(1:10), effect = c(4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, -1, -2, -3))
ggplot(gains, aes(person, effect, fill = effect > 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = cgray) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(gains$effect), linetype = "dashed", color = navy) +
  annotate("text", x = 10.45, y = 1.75, label = "ATE = 1", hjust = 1, color = navy, size = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = gold, `FALSE` = slate)) +
  labs(x = "ten imagined people", y = "gain") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

::: {.ask}
Belmont's justice: who gets the benefits of research, and who bears its burdens? For a policy, what would you need besides the ATE?
:::

::: {.source}
Wikipedia, Belmont Report.
:::

## Prediction and intervention

::: {.notes}
A model predicting Y from X can be equally accurate under all three. Acting on X changes Y only in the first.
:::

```{r three_dags, fig.height=2.9}
pics <- c("X causes Y", "Y causes X", "Z causes both")
nodes <- data.frame(panel = c(pics[1], pics[1], pics[2], pics[2], pics[3], pics[3], pics[3]),
                    name = c("X", "Y", "X", "Y", "Z", "X", "Y"),
                    x = c(0, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 2), y = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0))
edges <- data.frame(panel = c(pics[1], pics[2], pics[3], pics[3]),
                    from = c("X", "Y", "Z", "Z"), to = c("Y", "X", "X", "Y"))
nodes$panel <- factor(nodes$panel, levels = pics); edges$panel <- factor(edges$panel, levels = pics)
draw_dag(nodes, edges)
```

> "If we expect a model to also tell us what happens when we intervene on variables, then [...] models with equal predictive accuracy are no longer equivalent. We become responsible to choose one of them."

::: {.source}
Figure 1 of Loftus (2024), "Position: The Causal Revolution Needs Scientific Pragmatism," ICML.
:::

# Part 3: Confounding and adjustment

## A job-search course

::: {.notes}
Everyone writes something before the next slide. A press release would say 28 points.
:::

A job center refers some of the 1,000 people registered with it to a job-search course. Everyone referred attends, and nobody else does. Six months later:

| | attended | did not attend |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1,000 people | 320 of 500 in work (64%) | 180 of 500 in work (36%) |

::: {.ask}
How much does the course raise the chance of being in work? Write down a number, or what else you would need to know.
:::

## Draw the graph

::: {.notes}
Pairs, three minutes. Take two graphs from the room, one with a variable nobody measured, such as motivation, if anyone added one. Ask what else the 28 points needs besides the arrow: no arrows from worked last year into both.
:::

```{r course_blank, fig.height=1.7, fig.alt="Three boxes and no arrows: worked last year at the top, attended at the bottom left, in work at the bottom right."}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("worked last year", "attended", "in work"),
                    x = c(1.35, 0, 2.7), y = c(1, 0, 0), panel = ""),
         data.frame(from = character(0), to = character(0), panel = character(0)),
         boxes = TRUE, text_size = 6,
         xlim = c(-1.2, 3.9), ylim = c(-0.25, 1.25))
```

::: {.ask}
A press release says the course raises the chance of being in work by 28 percentage points.

1. Draw the arrow the press release needs.
2. Add arrows, from worked last year or any other variable you think matters, that would make attenders look better even if the course did nothing.
:::

## The job center: one graph

::: {.notes}
One answer among several. The arrows from working last year into both attending and being in work are what make attenders look better. If a pair added motivation, keep it: it is the U on the last slide of this part.
:::

```{r course_words, fig.height=1.7, fig.alt="The same three boxes with arrows: from worked last year to attended and to in work, and a gold arrow from attended to in work."}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("worked last year", "attended", "in work"),
                    x = c(1.35, 0, 2.7), y = c(1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("worked last year", "worked last year", "attended"),
                    to = c("attended", "in work", "in work")),
         highlight = "attended in work", boxes = TRUE, text_size = 6,
         xlim = c(-1.2, 3.9), ylim = c(-0.25, 1.25))
```

The gold arrow is the claim that the course helps people find work. The two black arrows can produce a difference between attenders and non-attenders without it.

## The rows

::: {.notes}
The center refers people who worked last year more readily: 80% against 20%. Within each row, 10 points.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
::: {.small}
| | attended ($X = 1$) | did not ($X = 0$) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| worked last year ($Z = 1$), 500 | 280 of 400 in work (70%) | 60 of 100 (60%) |
| did not ($Z = 0$), 500 | 40 of 100 in work (40%) | 120 of 400 (30%) |
| total, 1,000 | 320 of 500 in work (64%) | 180 of 500 (36%) |
:::
:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
```{r course_dag, fig.width=3.2, fig.height=2.6}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("Z", "X", "Y"), x = c(1, 0, 2), y = c(1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("Z", "Z", "X"), to = c("X", "Y", "Y")))
```
:::
::::

$Z$ = worked last year, $X$ = attended the course, $Y$ = in work six months later.

## The adjustment formula

::: {.notes}
Intervening deletes the arrow from Z to X; Z keeps its distribution. Ten points.
:::

$Z$ worked last year, $X$ attended, $Y$ in work. $do(X := 1)$ deletes the arrow $Z \to X$, and $Z$ keeps its distribution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[Y \mid do(X := 1)] &= \sum_z E[Y \mid X = 1, Z = z]\,P(Z = z) \\
&= 0.7 \times 0.5 + 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.55 \\
E[Y \mid do(X := 0)] &= 0.6 \times 0.5 + 0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.45
\end{aligned}
$$

The average treatment effect is $0.10$.

::: {.leave}
$P(Y = y \mid do(X := x)) = \sum_z P(Y = y \mid X = x, Z = z)\,P(Z = z)$ when $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion (later in the lecture), and every value of $Z$ includes people with $X = x$.
:::

## The observed comparison

::: {.notes}
The same rows, weighted by who attended. The extra 18 points: the referral sends people who would more often find work anyway.
:::

$Z$ worked last year, $X$ attended, $Y$ in work. Each row is weighted by its share of attenders, or of non-attenders:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) &= \frac{0.7 \times 400 + 0.4 \times 100}{500} = 0.64 \\
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) &= \frac{0.6 \times 100 + 0.3 \times 400}{500} = 0.36
\end{aligned}
$$

Attenders come mostly from the $Z = 1$ row, where more people find work whether or not they attend.

## Referral at random

::: {.notes}
Alone, two minutes. The answer is on the next slide.
:::

Same people, same rows. The center now refers half of each row, chosen at random; everyone referred attends, and nobody else does.

::: {.ask}
Compute the share in work you would expect among those who attended, and among those who did not. Compare the difference with the average treatment effect.
:::

## Randomization

::: {.notes}
Randomizing deletes the arrow into X in the world, including arrows from variables nobody measured.
If some refuse what they are offered, comparing the arms as assigned gives the effect of the offer.
:::

Half of each row attends, chosen at random. The shares to expect:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) &= 0.5 \times 0.7 + 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.55 \\
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) &= 0.5 \times 0.6 + 0.5 \times 0.3 = 0.45
\end{aligned}
$$

The difference to expect is $0.55 - 0.45 = 0.10$, the average treatment effect. Any one randomization gives a difference near $0.10$, and a different random draw would give a slightly different number.

> "The goal of a randomized controlled trial is to break natural inclination."

::: {.source}
fairmlbook, chapter 5, "Randomization."
:::

## The backdoor criterion

::: {.notes}
Pearl's two conditions; the reading cites him. Blocking is defined here for forks and chains; the reading says how colliders behave. The mediator is the first condition's case.
:::

A backdoor path from $X$ to $Y$ starts with an arrow into $X$: here, $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$.

$Z$ satisfies the **backdoor criterion** if

1. no variable in $Z$ is a descendant of $X$, and
2. $Z$ blocks every backdoor path from $X$ to $Y$.

A path through a fork or a chain is blocked by conditioning on the variable in the middle.

> Controlling for a mediator "will eliminate some of the causal influence of $X$ on $Y$."

::: {.source}
The criterion: Pearl (2009), *Causality*, as cited in fairmlbook, chapter 5. The quotation: fairmlbook, chapter 5, "Confounding."
:::

## Unobserved confounding

::: {.notes}
My graph against a colleague's. Same data, both fit. The choice of adjustment set is a claim about the world.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r unobs_dag, fig.width=3.6, fig.height=3}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("Z", "U", "X", "Y"), x = c(0.4, 1.6, 0, 2), y = c(1.1, 1.1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("Z", "Z", "U", "U", "X"), to = c("X", "Y", "X", "Y", "Y")),
         dashed = c("U X", "U Y"))
```
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
$U$: something unmeasured, such as motivation, that pushes people onto the course and into work.

Under the graph without $U$, adjusting for $Z$ gives the effect. Under this one, the back door through $U$ stays open, and the 10 points probably overstates the effect.

The data on $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ fit both graphs.
:::
::::

## Lenses this week

::: {.notes}
Each lens, what it referred to this week. Then the question on the next slide.
:::

- **Which comparison gets reported?** Attenders against non-attenders, overall or within rows. The average effect, or the effects within groups defined before treatment.
- **You have to choose, so choose, and defend it.** The adjustment set follows from a graph you drew. The backdoor criterion says which sets are valid given the graph. "Pretending it was forced is its own failure."

...and why?
